content: High costs associated with laboratory tests and other services can deter individuals from utilizing healthcare services, even when they are available. In the United States, economic challenges make long-acting injectable cabotegravir (CAB-LA) inaccessible for many individuals. In countries like Thailand, Lebanon, and Indonesia, where discussing sexual health is considered taboo, individuals may prefer free condoms over paid services to avoid disclosing their sexual practices. In high-income countries, it remains unclear whether CAB-LA will be covered by insurance or supported by adequate donor or project funding, especially in the absence of generic alternatives. Public health systems that currently fund generic PrEP drugs may find CAB-LA prohibitively expensive, limiting its availability to clients who can afford private healthcare. This concern has been raised in various countries, except those heavily reliant on project funding. In countries like Spain, Indonesia, Lebanon, Mexico, Guatemala, Poland, and Switzerland, there is concern that PrEP, including CAB-LA, may suffer from a flavor of the month effect, where initial funding for new priorities diminishes after a few years. In Lebanon and Ukraine, the high cost of CAB-LA could worsen existing stockout issues. In Zambia, Namibia, and Uganda, the cost of laboratory tests required for initiation is unaffordable for most clients, and in some countries, these tests are unavailable. Across regions, the anticipated high cost of CAB-LA suggests it may be better targeted toward individuals who struggle with adherence or have unstable lives. In Myanmar, transportation to clinics for injections and lost wages due to time away from work are additional barriers. In Australia, even if CAB-LA is approved in Europe, its availability in settings where PrEP is free will depend on negotiating acceptable pricing within national procurement frameworks. Questions about the added value of CAB-LA compared to daily oral PrEP remain. In the United States, the lack of a national PrEP program or guidance means resources are often focused on HIV/STI testing and treatment, with reliance on external guidelines. In Indonesia, restrictive national health policies limit PrEP access to local residents, affecting CAB-LA availability. In Mexico, national approval processes could delay CAB-LA's use in public health facilities by up to two years after WHO recommendations. In Thailand, concerns about detecting recent HIV infections may necessitate starting clients on daily oral PrEP before transitioning to CAB-LA. In Spain, questions have been raised about whether all current testing requirements, such as renal function and hepatitis screening, are necessary for CAB-LA. Additionally, there is limited knowledge about drug interactions for clients who use substances like chemsex drugs. In Nepal, access to advanced testing like NAT or viral load testing is limited, and government labs resist using expensive reagents for HIV-negative clients. WHO guidance on testing requirements for CAB-LA initiation is urgently needed. In the United States, viral load testing faces challenges such as reagent shortages, machine breakdowns, and transportation issues. In Nepal, the cost of CAB-LA is too high for most clients. In Ukraine, Indonesia, and the United States, the lack of public sector financing for PrEP in state facilities poses a significant threat to service expansion. In Australia, aversion to injections may deter some clients, necessitating the continued availability of daily oral PrEP. Clinical trial data indicate that injection site pain from CAB-LA is mild and temporary, but fear of this pain may deter new users. In Myanmar and Lebanon, human resource constraints, compounded by COVID-19-related responsibilities, may limit the ability to meet increased demand for CAB-LA. Across regions, reluctance to receive clinical services from non-physicians and criminalization of homosexuality in some countries further complicate service delivery. In high-volume clinics, the current model of care struggles to accommodate the demands of oral PrEP and HIV treatment. Delivering CAB-LA on a two-monthly schedule with testing requirements may be nearly impossible without additional staffing. In the UK and Australia, staffing shortages and logistical challenges could hinder CAB-LA delivery, especially with increased uptake. In some settings, anti-vaccine or anti-medication sentiments, often fueled by social media, may affect CAB-LA uptake. In Australia, PrEP services have primarily focused on men who have sex with men (MSM) and transgender women, but cisgender women also need to be included in marketing and information campaigns. In Thailand, misinformation among clients and providers highlights the need for more education. In Africa, where PrEP services are targeted at key populations like MSM and transgender women, provider reluctance to offer PrEP is common, requiring stronger advocacy and guidance from WHO. In some lowand middle-income countries, refrigeration requirements for CAB-LA are a barrier, though this may stem from confusion with other injectable treatments. In Myanmar, civil unrest and COVID-19 lockdowns have disrupted PrEP delivery, making adherence difficult. In Lebanon, overlapping crises such as economic instability and political unrest have made adherence to PrEP increasingly challenging. Hesitancy toward new products like CAB-LA may require creative knowledge-sharing to build public confidence. In Zimbabwe, high-volume clinics with thousands of ART clients may only be able to offer CAB-LA to a small percentage of eligible individuals. In Thailand, the time required for PrEP services, including testing, counseling, and injections, is a significant challenge in high-volume settings. Globally, updated WHO recommendations are needed to support advocacy, funding, and adoption of CAB-LA by ministries of health. Training for service providers on counseling, administration, monitoring, and safe discontinuation of CAB-LA is critical. In Thailand, eligibility considerations should focus on actual sexual behaviors rather than labels for gender identity or sexual orientation. In high HIV prevalence settings, sexually active individuals with multiple partners should be offered PrEP. In the United States, some providers prioritize CAB-LA for clients most at risk or those who decline daily PrEP due to privacy concerns. A blended approach, where clients use oral PrEP and injectable CAB-LA interchangeably based on their needs, may also be effective. In settings reliant on project funding, government buy-in is essential for sustainable PrEP services. In Switzerland, extending the frequency of CAB-LA injections to three months and transitioning to subcutaneous administration could be transformative. In summary, while CAB-LA offers significant potential for HIV prevention, its implementation faces numerous barriers, including cost, infrastructure, staffing, stigma, and policy challenges. Addressing these barriers will require coordinated efforts, including updated guidelines, training, advocacy, and innovative service delivery models.
